On the downside, a surprise macroeconomic data release — such as a hotter-than-expected inflation print or a sharp deterioration in employment figures — could trigger a rapid repricing of risk assets well beyond the lower bounds, particularly at the 1-month horizon. Geopolitical shocks, credit market stress, or an unexpected policy shift from a major central bank could similarly produce tail outcomes. On the upside, a strongly positive earnings surprise, an unexpected dovish pivot, or a broad risk-on rally driven by improving economic sentiment could push the price above the upper bounds of the intervals.

It is worth noting that these intervals represent 90% confidence ranges, meaning there is still a meaningful 10% probability of outcomes falling outside them across all three horizons. Financial markets are prone to fat-tailed distributions, and in practice extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. Anyone acting on these forecasts should treat the interval bounds not as hard limits but as guideposts, recognizing that truly unexpected events — by definition — are underrepresented in any probabilistic model built on historical patterns.
